topicTitle: Architectural Software Patterns in Native JavaScript

lessons.title: Creational Design Patterns: Factory, Singleton, Builder
lessons.description: Control how objects are created — factories produce flexible objects, singletons enforce uniqueness, builders construct complex ones.

sections.heading: Factory pattern
list: A function that creates and returns objects without using 'new'
Decouples object creation from the calling code
Can return different types based on input
Simplifies complex object creation logic

sections.heading: Singleton pattern
list: Ensures only one instance of a class exists
Provides a global access point to that instance
Use for: database connections, configuration, caches
Module-level variables in JavaScript are natural singletons

sections.heading: Builder pattern
list: Constructs complex objects step by step
Each step returns the builder for chaining
Separates construction from representation
Useful for objects with many optional parameters

codeExamples.heading: Three creational patterns
explanation: Factory: a function that creates different object types based on input.
Singleton: ensures only one instance exists via static method.
Builder: step-by-step construction with method chaining.
Each pattern solves a specific object creation problem.

practice.task: Implement a Factory that creates different notification types (email, SMS, push) based on user preference.
hints: Each type has different properties: to, phone, token.

keyTakeaways: Factory: creates objects without using 'new' — decouples creation from usage.
Singleton: ensures only one instance exists — use for shared resources.
Builder: constructs complex objects step by step with method chaining.
Choose the pattern based on your specific creation requirements.
lessons.challenge: Build a configuration manager using the Builder pattern that validates settings at each step.

lessons.title: Structural Design Patterns: Adapter, Proxy, Decorator
lessons.description: Structure objects and classes into larger combinations — adapters bridge interfaces, proxies control access, decorators add behavior.

sections.heading: Adapter pattern
sections.list: Converts one interface to another that the client expects.

sections.heading: Proxy pattern
sections.list: Controls access to another object — add logging, validation or caching.

sections.heading: Decorator pattern
sections.list: Adds behavior to objects dynamically without modifying their class.

codeExamples.heading: Three structural patterns
explanation: Adapter: wraps an old interface to match what the client expects.
Proxy: intercepts operations for logging, validation or caching.
Decorator: wraps a function to add behavior without changing it.
All three modify objects without changing their core implementation.
codeExamples.output:
> Singleton: same instance
> Factory: new instance each time
> Module: exports object

practice.task: Create a caching Proxy that caches the results of expensive function calls.
hints: Use a Proxy with a get trap.
Check if the result is cached before computing.
Store results in a Map keyed by arguments.

keyTakeaways: Adapter: converts one interface to another — bridges incompatible APIs.
Proxy: controls access to an object — add logging, validation or caching.
Decorator: adds behavior dynamically without modifying the original class.
All three follow the Open/Closed Principle — open for extension, closed for modification.
lessons.challenge: Build a rate-limiting Proxy that allows only N function calls per second.

lessons.title: Behavioral Design Patterns: Observer/PubSub, Strategy, Command
lessons.description: Manage communication and algorithms between objects — observers notify, strategies vary, commands encapsulate.

sections.heading: Observer/PubSub
sections.list: Objects subscribe to events and are notified when they occur — the foundation of event-driven architecture.

sections.heading: Strategy pattern
sections.list: Swap algorithms at runtime — pass different functions to achieve different behaviors.

sections.heading: Command pattern
sections.list: Encapsulate actions as objects — enables undo, redo and command queuing.

codeExamples.heading: Three behavioral patterns
explanation: PubSub: decouples publishers from subscribers via an event bus.
Strategy: swap algorithms by passing different functions.
Command: encapsulate actions as objects with execute/undo.
Each pattern handles communication and behavior differently.

practice.task: Implement a PubSub system with on, emit and off methods. Use it to decouple a form submission from multiple handlers.
hints: on(event, fn) subscribes; off(event, fn) unsubscribes; emit(event, data) notifies.
Store listeners in an object keyed by event name.
Emit calls all registered listeners for that event.

keyTakeaways: PubSub: decouples event producers from consumers — foundation of event-driven architecture.
Strategy: swap algorithms at runtime by passing different functions.
Command: encapsulate actions as objects — enables undo, redo and queuing.
Choose the pattern based on your communication and behavior requirements.
lessons.challenge: Build a complete undo/redo system for a text editor using the Command pattern.

lessons.title: Frontend Architecture: Store Pattern & Unidirectional Data Flow
lessons.description: Manage application state with a centralized store and unidirectional data flow — the foundation of Redux and similar architectures.

sections.heading: Store pattern
list: Single source of truth for application state
State is modified only through defined actions
Components read from the store and dispatch actions
Predictable state changes enable time-travel debugging

sections.heading: Unidirectional data flow
list: State flows down: store → components
Events flow up: components → actions → store → components
No two-way binding — data flows in one direction
Makes state changes predictable and debuggable

codeExamples.heading: Simple store implementation
explanation: The store holds the single source of truth for application state.
dispatch sends actions to the reducer — the only way to change state.
The reducer is a pure function: (state, action) => newState.
subscribe lets components react to state changes.

practice.task: Implement a simple store with getState, dispatch and subscribe. Use it to manage a counter with increment, decrement and reset actions.
hints: Reducer handles INCREMENT, DECREMENT and RESET actions.
Subscribe to log state changes on each dispatch.

keyTakeaways: The Store pattern provides a single source of truth for application state.
State changes only happen through dispatched actions and reducers.
Unidirectional data flow makes state changes predictable and debuggable.
This is the foundation of Redux, Vuex and similar state management libraries.
lessons.challenge: Build a complete todo app using the store pattern with add, toggle, delete and filter actions — all rendered to the DOM.
